summary: Describes using the HMAC algorithm with RIPEMD-160 as an authentication mechanism in IPsec ESP and AH. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A secret-key stamp checks that an IP packet is real and unchanged. This describes one particular stamp recipe for that job.

questions: why is the hmac authenticator truncated to 96 bits
what key length does hmac-ripemd-160-96 use
how does ripemd-160 work with esp and ah
subtitle: How to use HMAC with the RIPEMD-160 hash to authenticate IPsec packets, with a 96-bit tag and a 160-bit key.

tldr.problem: IPsec's ESP and AH need a keyed way to prove that a packet is authentic and was not modified in transit, and each hash-based option has to be pinned down exactly so implementations interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The memo plugs the RIPEMD-160 hash into the HMAC framework, keeps only the first 96 bits of the 160-bit result as the authenticator, and fixes the key length at 160 bits.
tldr.outcome: Implementations get one precise recipe for HMAC-RIPEMD-160-96, giving data origin authentication and integrity protection when only the two endpoints know the key.

today: RFC 2857 is a Proposed Standard from June 2000. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This Memo Specifies
sections.content:
RFC 2857 describes how to use HMAC together with the RIPEMD-160 hash as a keyed authentication mechanism inside the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and Authentication Header (AH). The stated goal of HMAC-RIPEMD-160-96 is to ensure that a packet is authentic and cannot be modified in transit.

HMAC is a secret key algorithm, so what it proves depends on who knows the key. If only the source and destination know the key and the HMAC is correct, that shows the HMAC must have been added by the source. That gives both data origin authentication and data integrity between the two parties.

The memo does not describe how ESP or AH work overall. It refers readers to the ESP and AH specifications and to the IP Security Document Roadmap for the other components.
sections.eli5: Imagine two friends who share a secret handshake. If a letter carries the right handshake mark, you know your friend wrote it and nobody changed it on the way.

sections.title: Algorithm and Mode
sections.content:
The RIPEMD-160 algorithm itself is defined elsewhere, and HMAC is defined in RFC 2104. HMAC is a framework that lets different hash algorithms be inserted, and this memo inserts RIPEMD-160.

HMAC-RIPEMD-160-96 works on 64-byte blocks of data. Padding is part of the RIPEMD-160 algorithm and is needed only to compute the authenticator value. The padding MUST NOT be included in the packet.

The computation produces a 160-bit value. For ESP and AH, an implementation MUST support truncating it to the first 96 bits. The sender stores the truncated value in the authenticator field. The receiver computes the whole 160-bit value and compares only the first 96 bits with the stored field. No other authenticator lengths are supported.

The 96-bit length was chosen because it is the default authenticator length in the AH specification and meets the security requirements in RFC 2104.
sections.eli5: The recipe makes a long stamp, but only the first part of it is written on the packet. The receiver makes the whole stamp again and checks that the first part matches.

sections.title: Performance
sections.content:
The memo quotes the observation that HMAC performance is essentially that of the underlying hash function. It says the RIPEMD-160 specification provides some performance analysis, but that no detailed analysis of HMAC combined with RIPEMD-160 had been done at the time of writing.

It also points to an implementation modification outlined in RFC 2104 that can improve per-packet performance without affecting interoperability.
sections.eli5: Making the stamp takes about as long as the hash underneath it. There is also a shortcut that makes it quicker without changing the result.

sections.title: Keying Material
sections.content:
HMAC-RIPEMD-160-96 is a secret key algorithm. RFC 2104 does not fix a key length, but for ESP and AH a fixed key length of 160 bits MUST be supported, and other key lengths SHALL NOT be supported. The choice follows RFC 2104: keys shorter than the authenticator length weaken security, and longer keys do not add much strength.

The 160-bit key MUST come from a strong pseudo-random function. Implementors are pointed to RFC 1750 for the requirements. No weak keys for HMAC were specified when the memo was written, but the text says that does not mean none exist. If weak keys are found, they must be rejected and replacement keys or a newly negotiated Security Association requested.

To get data origin authentication, the key distribution mechanism must hand out unique keys and give them only to the parties in the communication. Deriving the key from keying material is the same for manual and automatic key management.

The memo notes that frequent rekeying is still cryptographically prudent, but that no recommended key lifetimes for HMAC-RIPEMD existed yet. They were to be added to a revised version when available.
sections.eli5: The shared secret must be exactly the right size and picked by a good random process, like a lock combination nobody could guess. Only the two people talking should ever get a copy.

sections.title: Interaction with ESP Ciphers
sections.content: The memo says there were no known issues that prevent HMAC-RIPEMD-160-96 from being used with any specific cipher algorithm in ESP. In other words, the authenticator can be paired with whichever encryption algorithm an ESP user picks.
sections.eli5: The stamp works no matter which secret code you use to scramble the message inside.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of HMAC-RIPEMD-160-96 rests on the strength of HMAC and, to a lesser degree, on RIPEMD-160. At the time of writing there were no known practical cryptographic attacks against RIPEMD-160. The memo adds that RIPEMD-160 was not designed as a keyed hash, whereas HMAC had that goal from the start.

Truncating the hash can add security, and specifications that include HMAC are strongly encouraged to do it. Because HMAC is a framework, RIPEMD-160 could be replaced by another hash such as SHA-1.

As with any cryptographic algorithm, strength also depends on a correct implementation, secure key management, a strong secret key and correct behavior on every participating system. The memo points to a separate RFC with test vectors and example code for checking HMAC-RIPEMD-160-96 implementations.

It also repeats the claim from RFC 2104 that a birthday attack on a 64-byte block hash would be infeasible unless the underlying hash had collisions after processing 2**30 blocks, and a hash that weak would generally be considered unusable.
sections.eli5: The stamp is only as good as the recipe, the secret and the people following the steps. Test examples are published so builders can check they got it right.

items.title: Stored value
items.text: First 96 bits, in the authenticator field.
